intro: “Fürchtenmachen” (Frightening) is No. 11 of Schumann’s Kinderszenen, Op. 15. A soft tune on the piano is followed by a sudden fast passage and then by sharp accented chords.

sections.label: A · Soft theme in semitone steps
B · Schneller, staccato chords
sections.mNote: Schneller, pianissimo; the short passage is repeated.

sections.label: A′ · The tune and sudden shocks
sections.mNote: Sforzando chords interrupt the returning tune.

sections.label: A″ · The tune in G major
sections.mNote: A quiet ending, after the surprises.

cues.title: Opening bars, repeated B
cues.text: A B recurs in the melody. Below it, sharps and naturals move the inner parts by semitones. Schumann marks the opening pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, pp. 16–17, opening eight bars: repeated B in the melody, chromatic inner parts and pianissimo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schneller passage
cues.text: In the passage marked Schneller (faster), the right hand plays short chords while the left runs up and down, still pianissimo. Later Schumann adds sforzando marks to the returning tune.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 16: Schneller, pianissimo and staccato writing; the later four-bar interruption has forte and repeated sforzandos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Liszt’s open letter to Berlioz, 1839
cues.text: In October 1839 Liszt praised Kinderszenen in an open letter to Berlioz, calling Schumann “a poet full of feeling and a great musician”. Schumann kept the cutting in his scrapbook and marked the closing paragraph in red.
cues.evidence: Liszt to Hector Berlioz, Revue et Gazette musicale, 24 October 1839; Schumann’s annotated cutting described in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 10. Translation from the catalogue’s German quotation. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: G major cadence to the first Schneller
transitions.from: A · Soft theme in semitone steps
transitions.how: The opening phrase closes in G major. Over the next passage Schumann writes Schneller, and the dynamic stays pianissimo. The right hand plays short chords, and in the gaps between them the left hand plays fast figures. Both hands play lightly and detached.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 16, close of the first strain and first Schneller passage.

transitions.title: Return of the opening B
transitions.to: A′ · The tune and sudden shocks
transitions.how: The repeated G major Schneller section ends. The melody returns to the opening B, with chromatic inner notes beneath it. A few bars later the soft tune is interrupted by a forte passage with repeated sforzandos.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 16, end of the first Schneller repeat, returning opening phrase and following forte interruption.

transitions.title: Return of the Schneller passage
transitions.from: A′ · The tune and sudden shocks
transitions.how: The tune closes in G major, and the quick passage returns. Schneller and pianissimo are marked again above the staccato chords. The left hand plays fast figures beneath them, and a repeat sign sends both hands back through the passage a second time.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 17, second Schneller passage and its repeat signs.

transitions.title: Final return of the opening tune
transitions.to: A″ · The tune in G major
transitions.how: The short chords stop, and the opening tune returns over its chromatic accompaniment for the final eight bars. This time it continues to the end without the sforzando interruption. The bass and the closing chord end on G major.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 17, final eight-bar return and G-major closing chord.

fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
